On the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has taken another step toward the long-term vision of turning the iPhone into "a single slab of glass": embedding the Face ID module beneath the display.

Achieving a Face ID component that doesn't show through the screen, while also not affecting display quality in that area, requires some remarkably delicate engineering……

Jony Ive once described his long-term vision for the iPhone's design as "a single slab of glass," and although he has since left the company, that goal has lived on. Apple ultimately wants to embed all the technologies currently occupying screen real estate—including Face ID and the front camera—entirely beneath the display.

The iPhone 18 Pro becomes the first model to achieve the former, but the process is far from simple. Face ID requires the TrueDepth module to both emit and receive infrared light, and infrared cannot pass through display pixels.

Apple had to create gaps between the pixels large enough for infrared to pass through, without causing any visible degradation to the screen. To achieve this, Apple's engineers redesigned an entirely new pixel arrangement, widening the gaps without significantly compromising the pixels' ability to display content.

iFixit has already shown this pixel arrangement under a microscope, and Apple confirmed to me that the overall pixel density across the entire module area is cut in half. That would normally create a second problem: halving the pixel density would likely make that region of the screen noticeably dimmer, so Apple compensated by boosting the brightness of those pixels. They also appear to have added an infrared filter to block visible light from passing through the gaps, further hiding the component.

The results are quite remarkable. In everyday use, even staring at the screen up close, you simply cannot see the TrueDepth camera assembly at all. I tried macro photography across different screen colors and lighting conditions and couldn't capture it. Of course, that doesn't mean it's completely undetectable—iFixit's microscope images clearly show it—but in daily use, you would absolutely never notice it.

This breakthrough currently allows the Dynamic Island to shrink, which in turn enables support for displaying three Live Activities simultaneously instead of two. On some future iPhone model, the front camera will also be hidden beneath the display. The technology exists today, but the trade-offs in image quality are still beyond what Apple is willing to accept. That problem will be solved eventually, though.
